title: Tunisia's pesticide use per hectare is low (0.83 kg/ha of cropland in 2024, about one third of the world average); the evidence of harm points to misuse in greenhouse vegetables, with residues above EU limits, unprotected workers and weak monitoring

rootCauses.cause: Product inefficacy leads growers to raise doses or application frequency, while labels and pre-harvest intervals are not followed

The 1992 plant protection law built a registration (homologation) system, but no systematic statistics are collected on pesticide use by crop or on health or environmental effects (the sources opened describe no residue-monitoring programme), and some substances banned in Europe stay on the market

author: TahaGHZ
excerpt: The brief framed pesticides as a problem of use, residues and regulation. Per-hectare use remains below the world average: FAOSTAT estimates Tunisian use at 0.83 kg of active ingredient per hectare of cropland in 2024…

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content: The brief framed pesticides as a problem of use, residues and regulation. Per-hectare use remains below the world average: FAOSTAT estimates Tunisian use at 0.83 kg of active ingredient per hectare of cropland in 2024, against 2.49 kg/ha worldwide, 0.87 in Northern Africa and 1.65 in Europe (SRC-TG-831). Total use was estimated at 4,047 t in 2024, the highest value in the series, including 2,533 t of fungicides (SRC-TG-831). Tunisia's intensity is close to the Northern Africa average and about one third of the world average. The evidence of harm is concentrated in intensive greenhouse vegetables. In Sousse in 2017, 20 harvest samples of tomato and chili pepper showed 7 exceedances of EU maximum residue limits, up to 26 times the limit. Worst-case chlorpyrifos intake from tomatoes reached 312% of the acute reference dose for children (SRC-TG-832). Workers rarely wear protection, and growers lack training (SRC-TG-832, SRC-TG-833).

sections.heading: Root causes
sections.content:
- **Practice in protected horticulture.** Tomato and chili pepper are sprayed many times up to harvest. The study links some product inefficacy to growers raising doses or spraying more often; it also reports that labels and pre-harvest intervals are not followed (SRC-TG-832). Only 8.3% of surveyed re-entry farm workers wore gloves (SRC-TG-832). These practices contribute to residue and worker-exposure risks.
- **Training and waste.** In an FAO survey of 1,174 farmers in Ben Arous, Nabeul and Monastir, relayed by Böll, 91% had no training on pesticide best practice and only 33% used protective equipment; 63% burned empty packaging outdoors and 30% left waste in nature (SRC-TG-833). The same report gives high PPE cost (no subsidy) and market unavailability as reasons for non-use.
- **Safe-use barriers (reported, tier B).** The same survey summary gives high PPE cost (no subsidy) and market unavailability as reasons for non-use, alongside training gaps and unsafe disposal (SRC-TG-833). The original survey was not opened, so these barriers are reported here, not presented as independently established root causes.
- **Regulation (past decision).** Law 92-72 of 3 August 1992 recast plant protection law and organised the pesticide sector. It bans the import, sale or distribution of any pesticide without registration or a provisional sales authorisation from the Minister of Agriculture (SRC-TG-834). The framework covers market entry, but monitoring is weak. The Toumi et al. study links the problems mainly to "regulation weaknesses, the lack of awareness and monitoring" (SRC-TG-832). Böll reports that no statistics on use by crop or on health and environmental effects are collected, and that pesticides banned in Europe remain on the Tunisian market (SRC-TG-833).

sections.heading: Evidence
sections.content:
- National volumes and intensity, with comparisons for 2024: Tunisia 0.83 kg/ha; world 2.49, Africa 0.83, Northern Africa 0.87 and Europe 1.65 (SRC-TG-831).
- Training: in the FAO 2019 survey relayed by Böll (1,174 farmers in Ben Arous, Nabeul and Monastir), 91% had no training on best practice (SRC-TG-833). For Tunisia's pesticide-use total, 1997 is flagged A; from 1998 onward values are E, I or X (SRC-TG-831).
- **Sources disagree:** Böll gives 4,161.2 t of pesticide imports in 2022 and an average use of 0.714 kg/ha (ANGeD, 2013) (SRC-TG-833). FAOSTAT gives 3,247 t of use and 0.66 kg/ha for 2022 (SRC-TG-831). Imports and use are different measures, and the Böll figure may be formulated product, so both are recorded. They agree that intensity is below 1 kg/ha.
- Residues, consumer intake and worker exposure: SRC-TG-832 (peer-reviewed; 20 fruit samples, 73 growers, Sousse, April 2017; EU MRLs as reference). Böll quotes the chlorpyrifos adult figure as 80%; the paper says 82% (SRC-TG-833, SRC-TG-832).
- Legal framework: SRC-TG-834.

sections.heading: Why confidence is what it is
sections.content: Low overall. The volume comparison relies on FAOSTAT estimates from 1998 onward, not official Tunisian values. The misuse and residue part rests on one small peer-reviewed study (20 samples, one governorate, one week, EU limits) and on a tier B policy paper relaying surveys that were not opened. Low use per hectare across all cropland can hide high use on a small area of greenhouses; the data needed to show how use is distributed do not exist in the sources opened. FAOSTAT's 2024 estimate is the highest in its series, though flags and estimation limit certainty about the level. The concentrated-misuse claim is plausible but thinly sourced.

sections.heading: Links to other sectors
sections.content: Water: the 2024 national plant genetic resources report lists irrational pesticide use among threats to biodiversity (SRC-TG-828), but no water contamination data were opened. None found for energy.

sections.heading: Leads for phase 2
sections.content:
- Pesticide registration (homologation) under law 92-72 and decree 92-2246 (SRC-TG-834, SRC-TG-833): https://faolex.fao.org/docs/pdf/tun11737.pdf
- Mandatory import inspection of agricultural pesticides, decree 94-1744 (SRC-TG-833).
- Distributing protective equipment with pesticide purchases, proposed by workers (SRC-TG-832).
- Biological control studies cited by Böll: mass trapping of the carob moth, entomopathogenic nematodes (SRC-TG-833).
- ILO Convention C184 on Safety and Health in Agriculture, not ratified by Tunisia according to Böll (SRC-TG-833).

sections.heading: Verification
sections.content:
Use, import, residue and legal figures were checked against the cited sources.

**Independent review, 21 November 2026:** pass after corrections. Checked in the originals: FAOSTAT pesticides (SRC-TG-831; checked in the saved transcript of the bulk CSV rows, items 1357, 1331, elements 5157 and 5159, 2010-2024, because the bulk file and API could not be fetched live); Toumi et al. 2018 (SRC-TG-832) abstract p.127, methods and results p.131-132; Böll 2025 (SRC-TG-833) paras. 1-6; Law 92-72 (SRC-TG-834) arts. 1 and 16. Corrections: root cause 2 no longer says there is "no systematic monitoring of use by crop, residues or health effects"; it now says no systematic statistics are collected on use by crop or on health or environmental effects, and that the sources opened describe no residue-monitoring programme (Böll does not mention residues in that sentence). Independent teammate sign-off is outstanding; reviewer and author share the TahaGHZ identity, so the record is not validated.

Article 4, question 2A, p. 3:

> Loi nº 99-42 relative aux semences, plants et obtentions végétales. Cette loi fixe les modalités de production, de multiplication, d'importation, de commercialisation des plants, des semences et des obtentions végétales ainsi les modalités de protection des droits s'y rapportants.

> · Décret nº 2000-1282, fixant la forme du catalogue officiel, les procédures d'inscription des variétés végétales et les conditions d'inscription des semences et plants obtenus récemment sur la liste d'attente. 2000-06-13
> · Décret nº 2000-101, fixant la classification des semences et plants, leur production et multiplication, les normes générales de leur stockage, emballage et étiquetage, le contrôle de leur qualité et état sanitaire et leur commercialisation. 2000-01-18
> · Décret nº 2000-102, fixant la composition et les modalités de fonctionnement de la commission technique des semences, plants et obtentions végétales. 2000-01-18

English gloss: Law 99-42 on seeds, plants and plant varieties sets the rules for production, multiplication, import and marketing of seeds and plants and for protecting related rights.

Article 5, question 6, p. 5:

> La diversité biologique en Tunisie est confrontée à plusieurs menaces naturelles ou anthropiques. Les menaces de nature anthropique, qui pèsent lourd sur la diversité biologique, englobe l'urbanisation, l'appauvrissement de la palette de variétés cultivées, l'intensification des cultures et les utilisations non rationnelles de pesticides, la dégradation des espaces steppiques et des forêts, etc.

English gloss: Human threats to biodiversity include urbanisation, the narrowing of the range of cultivated varieties, crop intensification, irrational pesticide use, and degradation of steppe and forest.

p. 5:

> L'évaluation de l'érosion génétique n'est pas souvent standardisée selon des critères internationaux et souffre d'un manque d'informations sur les états initiaux ;

English gloss: Assessment of genetic erosion is often not standardised to international criteria and lacks baseline information.

p. 6 (oases):

> Dans les oasis de Kébili, la dominance de la variété Deglet Nour rend une majorité des variétés communes de datte en situation menacée et sont de plus en plus rares.

English gloss: In the Kebili oases, the dominance of Deglet Nour puts most common date varieties under threat; they are increasingly rare.

Article 9 (farmers' rights), question 19B, p. 13: the field asking for details of measures taken to protect farmers' rights, including the right to save, use, exchange and sell farm-saved seed, is left empty (">>>" with no text).
resolvedSources.notes: Official country report submitted 19 November 2024 through the Treaty's online system; qualitative, no quantified erosion indicators. Classified tier B because it is a self-reported questionnaire, not statistics.

resolvedSources.title: Risk Assessment of Tunisian Consumers and Farm Workers Exposed to Residues after Pesticide Application in Chili Peppers and Tomatoes
resolvedSources.publisher: Tunisian Journal of Plant Protection 13(1): 127-143 (Toumi K., Joly L., Tarchoun N., Souabni L., Bouaziz M., Vleminckx C., Schiffers B.)
resolvedSources.extracts:
Abstract, p. 127:

> A questionnaire was addressed to a group of 73 market gardeners to better understand the local professional practices and to determine the main route of exposure to pesticide.

> The highest exposure of consumers was observed for chlorpyrifos residues on tomatoes (with 82% and 312% of the Acute Reference Dose (ARfD), for adults and children respectively).

> At the highest observed concentrations, 15 pesticide residues (active ingredients and metabolites) used in pepper greenhouses, and 9 in tomato crops, exceeded the Acceptable Operator Exposure Level (AOEL).

> Long task duration (8 h/day) after re-entry in greenhouse, limited access to personal protective equipment (PPE), lack of hygiene and bad habits (eating, drinking, or smoking at work) have also been observed and discussed as risk factors.

Introduction, p. 127:

> During cultivation, chili pepper and tomato require the use of a broad range of pesticides to prevent and control pests and diseases. Fruits and vegetables are sprayed several times and up to the final harvest.

Materials and methods, p. 128:

> A random sampling of tomatoes (10 samples) and chili peppers (10 samples) was carried out from 25 to 28 April 2017 in Sousse governorate, according to the guidelines of the European Directive 2002/63/EC

Results, p. 131 to 132:

> More than 20% have no idea about the recommended dosage of the PPPs and use them based on their experience or according to their supplier indications. The majority harvest their products without respect of the PHI, sometimes the day after treatment. Regarding security, 57 operators never wear Plant Protection Equipment (PPE) during mixing and loading or cleaning of the spray equipment.

> very few wear appropriate protective equipment such as gloves (8.3%), aprons (15%) or special clothing (22%).

(The 8.3% glove figure refers to farm workers re-entering treated greenhouses after treatment.)

> Problems are mainly linked to regulation weaknesses, the lack of awareness and monitoring, but also to the inefficacy of some PPP leading them to increase the dosage or application frequency.

> Seven MRL exceedances were reported: six exceedances in chili pepper (Table 1) and one exceedance for chlorpyrifos ethyl (insecticide) in tomatoes (Table 2). The MRL exceedances appeared particularly critical for propargite (chili pepper) and chlorpyrifos-ethyl (tomato) with concentration values respectively 20 (2000% of MRL) and 26 (2685% of MRL) times higher than the MRL values.

Tables 1 and 2 footnote:

> MRL and ARfD values from EU Pesticides database.

English gloss: In greenhouse tomato and chili pepper in Sousse (Sahel), 20 harvest samples (April 2017) showed 7 exceedances of EU maximum residue limits, up to 26 times the limit; worst-case consumer intake of chlorpyrifos reached 312% of the acute reference dose for children; few workers wear protective equipment; authors link problems to weak regulation, low awareness and monitoring.
resolvedSources.notes: Small sample (20 fruit samples, 73 growers, 20 glove samples), one governorate, one sampling week; not representative of national produce. MRLs are EU limits, not Tunisian limits.

resolvedSources.title: Tunisia: Pesticides governance - What should be known about pesticides in Tunisia
resolvedSources.publisher: Heinrich-Böll-Stiftung, Palestine and Jordan Office (author: Dr. Maroua Jerbi)
resolvedSources.extracts:
> In 2022, Tunisia imported 4,161.2 tonnes of pesticides, reflecting a significant 33 percent decrease from the previous year. This decline is largely due to reduced cultivated areas resulting from drought and water scarcity, alongside a general lack of awareness regarding the sever[ity]

> There is no policy in place for systematic collection of information and the updating of statistics on pesticide usage by crop, nor their harmful effects on human health or environmental contamination. According to the study conducted by the National Agency for Waste Management (ANGeD) in 2013, the average pesticide usage in Tunisia is estimated to be 0.714 kg/ha.

> Many dangerous pesticides that are banned in Europe are still available on the Tunisian market and are used by local farmers. In 2018, a national report from the Center for Innovation in Agriculture and Industry (IAAA), and which was conducted by CABI, identified 44 extremely hazardous active substances that were approved and shipped to Tunisia, including chlorpyrifos.

> The study covered three agricultural regions: Ben Arous, Nabeul, and Monastir, involving 1174 farmers. The study found that only 33 percent of the farmers surveyed 'used personal protective equipment (PPE)', while the majority (42 percent) had 'never worn it'.

> The study ultimately highlighted that a large percentage of the farmers surveyed (81 percent) had a low level of education (primary and secondary), and that 91 percent had not received training on best practices for pesticides use.

> Although they are aware of their importance, various reasons were cited for not using PPE, such as high costs (no subsidy scheme), unavailability on the market, bulkiness, or unsuitability due to high temperatures.

> This is evident from practices such as 'burning empty packaging outdoors' (63 percent), 'abandoning waste in nature' (30 percent), 'storing pesticide at homes' (22 percent), and frequently disregarding the recommended dosages and pre-harvest intervals.

> Law No. 92-72 of 3 August 1992, and its implementing decree No. 92-2246 of 28 December 1992,

> All agricultural pesticides are automatically inspected upon importation (decree No. 94-1744 of 22 August 1994) by laboratories accredited by the Ministry of Agriculture.

> Despite Tunisia being a member of the International Labour Organization (ILO), it has yet to ratify the ILO's Safety and Health in Agriculture Convention (C184).

> In 2019, a study revealed that controlling the carob worm (Ectomyelois ceratoniae), which attacks a wide range of host plants, was successfully managed using mass trapping techniques that reduced infestation rates in citrus orchards.

> Lastly, a 2023 study highlighted the use of entomopathogenic nematodes (EPNs) in conjunction with bacteria to control the wax moth (Galleria mellonella).

English gloss: Pesticide imports were 4,161.2 t in 2022, down 33%. No statistics on use by crop or on health and environmental effects are collected; ANGeD (2013) estimated average use at 0.714 kg/ha. Pesticides banned in Europe remain on sale; a 2018 CABI report found 44 highly hazardous active substances approved and shipped to Tunisia. In an FAO survey of 1,174 farmers, 33% used protective equipment, 42% never had, 91% had no training, 63% burned empty packaging and 30% left waste in nature. Imports are inspected by accredited laboratories (decree 94-1744). Tunisia has not ratified ILO C184. Studies cite mass trapping and nematodes as biological control options.
resolvedSources.notes: Policy paper by a foundation; it relays secondary studies (an FAO 2019 survey of 1,174 farmers, an ANGeD 2013 study, a CABI 2018 report) that were not opened here. Whether the import tonnage (4,161 t in 2022) is formulated product or active ingredient is not stated, so it is not directly comparable with FAOSTAT active-ingredient use (SRC-TG-831). The article misquotes the Toumi et al. (2018) chlorpyrifos figure as 80% (the paper says 82%, SRC-TG-832).

resolvedSources.title: Loi n° 92-72 du 3 août 1992 portant refonte de la législation relative à la protection des végétaux
resolvedSources.publisher: Republic of Tunisia (text hosted by FAOLEX)
resolvedSources.extracts:
Article premier:

> La présente loi fixe les dispositions générales relatives à la protection des végétaux et à l'organisation du secteur des pesticides à usage agricole.

Article 16:

> Sous réserve des dispositons de la législation en vigueur, il est interdit de fabriquer, d'importer, de formuler, de conditionner, de tenir, de transporter, de vendre, de distribuer tout produit presticide utilisé pour combattre les organismes nuisibles n'ayant pas fait l'objet d'une homologation ou autorisatin provisoire de vente délivre par le Ministre de l'Agriculture, après avis d'une commission technique dont la composition est fixée par décision du Ministre de l'Agriculture.

English gloss: The law sets the general rules for plant protection and organises the agricultural pesticide sector. Article 16 bans making, importing, formulating, packaging, holding, transporting, selling or distributing any pesticide without registration (homologation) or a provisional sales authorisation from the Minister of Agriculture, on the advice of a technical commission.
resolvedSources.notes: FAOLEX retyped text, not a JORT scan; typos are in the source ("dispositons", "presticide", "autorisatin"). It is signed "Tunis, le 3 août 1992". JORT issue and page were not shown in the opened document; legislation.tn returned HTTP 503 on 2026-11-21; iort.gov.tn answered but was not searched for this text. Type "official-statistics" is used for lack of a "legal-text" type in the template.
